sources.title: Diet of Theropithecus from 4 to 1 Ma in Kenya
supports: Isotope data showing Theropithecus brumpti was a committed C4 grass-grazing specialist in the same Turkana Basin landscape as Kenyanthropus platyops

sources.title: Isotopic evidence for dietary differences between two extinct baboon species from Swartkrans
supports: Isotope evidence that a giant contemporary baboon (Theropithecus oswaldi) at Swartkrans was a committed grass-grazing specialist while Paranthropus robustus kept a mixed diet despite having comparable chewing hardware

sources.title: Taphonomic analysis at Liang Bua reveals the behavioral and technological capabilities of Homo floresiensis
supports: Komodo dragon tooth marks concentrated on the meatiest Stegodon bones at Liang Bua, with Homo floresiensis cut marks confined to lower-value scraps — evidence of scavenging rather than primary carcass access
sources.qualityNote: Published July 3, 2026 — corroborated independently by CNN, National Geographic, Live Science, Sci.News and Gizmodo citing the same paper.

sources.title: The European saber-toothed cat (Homotherium latidens) found in the "Spear Horizon" at Schöningen (Germany)
supports: Bite/cut-mark sequencing shows hominins usually had primary carcass access over Homotherium at Schöningen, not the reverse; a saber-tooth humerus was reused as a stone-tool retoucher; the engineered spears may have doubled as defense against this rival predator

sources.title: Bears and humans, a Neanderthal tale. Reconstructing uncommon behaviors from zooarchaeological evidence in southern Europe
sources.authors: Romandini, Terlato, Nannini, Tagliacozzo, Benazzi & Peresani
supports: Cut marks on cave-bear and brown-bear bones at Rio Secco and Fumane caves (Italy) showing Neanderthals actively competed with bears for winter den shelter, including killing hibernating individuals

sources.title: East African uplift as a catalyst for Middle Miocene faunal transitions
supports: Climate modelling linking East African Rift uplift and falling CO2 to reduced forest cover and grassland expansion across the Middle-to-Late Miocene — a candidate explanation for the ~10-million-year African ape fossil gap between Ekembo and Nakalipithecus

sources.title: Comment on the Paleoenvironment of Ardipithecus ramidus
supports: A specialist rebuttal arguing Ardipithecus ramidus's Aramis habitat was predominantly open wooded grassland rather than closed woodland, based on soil-carbonate carbon isotopes — an active, unresolved dispute with the describing team's (White et al.) closed-woodland reading

sources.title: A complete skull from Dmanisi, Georgia, and the evolutionary biology of early Homo
supports: Dmanisi Skull 5 (546 cc braincase) found alongside much larger-brained individuals in one population, leading the describing team to argue Homo habilis, H. rudolfensis and early H. erectus may represent one variable, evolving lineage rather than separate species

sources.title: The bonobo genome compared with the chimpanzee and human genomes
supports: Genomic divergence dating chimpanzee/bonobo split to roughly 1-2 million years ago, coinciding with Congo River formation separating their ranges

sources.title: Perimortem fractures in Lucy suggest mortality from fall out of tall tree
supports: CT-scan evidence of perimortem compression fractures in the Lucy (AL 288-1) skeleton consistent with a fatal fall from height, most likely a tree — contested by other researchers who argue the breaks are post-mortem

sources.title: Human-like hand use in Australopithecus africanus
sources.authors: Skinner, Stephens, Tsegai, Foote, Nguyen, Gross, Pahr, Hublin & Kivell
supports: Trabecular (internal spongy) bone in africanus's thumb and palm shows a human-like loading pattern consistent with forceful, precision gripping, predating any confirmed stone-tool industry for this species

sources.title: 3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya
supports: Stone tools dated to 3.3 Ma, roughly 750,000 years older than Australopithecus garhi's butchered-bone layer and predating the genus Homo entirely, made by an unidentified non-Homo hominin

sources.title: The changing face of genus Homo
supports: Argument that Homo habilis's below-the-neck body proportions (short legs, long arms, small stature) are Australopithecus-like enough that the species arguably belongs in Australopithecus, not Homo

sources.title: New fossils from Koobi Fora in northern Kenya confirm taxonomic diversity in early Homo
supports: Juvenile partial face KNM-ER 62000, sharing rudolfensis's distinctive features at an immature size, supporting rudolfensis as a genuinely separate species from habilis rather than large-individual sexual variation

sources.title: The Endocast of MH1, Australopithecus sediba
supports: Synchrotron scan of sediba's braincase showing early frontal-lobe reorganization toward a human-like pattern despite a still-small brain — reorganization preceding size increase

sources.title: The evolution of modern human brain shape
supports: Homo sapiens braincases only reached the fully globular shape typical of living humans between ~100,000 and 35,000 years ago, well after early sapiens faces and brain size already looked modern

sources.title: Multiple Deeply Divergent Denisovan Ancestries in Papuans
supports: Modern Papuan/Melanesian populations carry the highest Denisovan ancestry of any living group, from at least two Denisovan populations separated 350,000+ years, implying an unfound Denisovan population in Southeast Asia/Wallacea
